newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Inquiry holds key to Australian bank mergers.
newsitem.headline: Inquiry holds key to Australian bank mergers.

text.p: A wide-ranging report into Australia's financial sector to be issued this week is expected to hold the key to mergers between the country's big four banks.

The government had instructed the inquiry that generated the report to examine issues facing not just banks but also other financial institutions such as insurers, whose clout has grown tremendously in recent years.
But analysts say the inquiry, headed by former businessman Stan Wallis, focussed on the traditional obsession of the Australian financial industry -- banking takeovers and mergers.
Treasurer Peter Costello ordered the inquiry in May 1996, saying the existing regulatory system had not been examined thoroughly since Australian financial markets were deregulated in the mid 1980s.
"I think the (proposed) regulatory changes are of modest significance in the short-medium term," said a banking analyst from a major Sydney brokerage firm. "The key issue is mergers."
Two forces are generally seen as pulling Australian banking in opposite directions.
One is that the country's biggest four banks are considered to be too small compared to enormous international competitors.
The other is a perception of inadequate competition, sharpened by Australians' historic hostility to banks.

To sustain competition, Canberra has banned mergers between the big four banks and the two biggest life insurance offices: National Australia Bank Ltd, Commonwealth Bank of Australia Ltd, Westpac Banking Corp, Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd, and National Mutual Holdings Ltd and soon-to-be-listed AMP Society.

Westpac on Thursday announced a deal to takeover the smaller Bank of Melbourne Ltd, but the government immediately said that its approval would depend on the policy it developed after examining the Wallis Inquiry report.

The anti-monopolies watchdog, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, has opposed mergers that would leave a state without a significant regional bank like the Bank of Melbourne, and says it would need evidence of changed circumstances before altering that stance.
But observers say that circumstances have changed in recent years: the life offices and a mass of smaller organisations have begun to offer such basic banking services as home loans.
The trend is expected to continue as telecoms companies and others move into financial services, probably on the Internet.
So some analysts say that if the Wallis report widens the notion of the market to include other organisations, it might see improved competition, easing resistance to mergers.
"I think big-bank mergers will eventuate and that we'll see them happen sooner rather than later," said one analyst.
The report also is expected to comment on the view that Australia could have bigger banks with no sacrifice of competition if it lifted its tight restrictions on foreign ownership of banks.

But analysts say that if local banks are unpopular among Australian voters, foreign-controlled banks would be viewed with great suspicion and the government might be unable to get such a change through parliament.
The report also is expected to address regulatory issues, notably deposit insurance.

At present, many bank customers assume that the government guarantees their deposits through the Reserve Bank. In fact, it does not, and the deposits are no safer than the bank itself, which the Reserve Bank supervises.
Analysts say the situation could be clarified by a government guarantee -- unlikely in an increasingly free-market economy -- or by introducing deposit insurance.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
